title: Membership Inference Attacks for Unseen Classes
claim: Under distribution shift to unseen classes, standard attacks collapse to baseline while our approach generalizes and retains much higher detection rates.
layout: 1 panel, grouped bar chart over 20 classes, legend on top
description: A single grouped bar chart. The x-axis lists 20 classes (0–19), and the y-axis is True Positive Rate from 0 to 0.08. Each class has four adjacent bars, listed in a legend at the top: Quantile Regression (purple), RMIA (red), LiRA (orange), and LOSS (green). The purple bars are usually the tallest, ranging from about 0.01 to 0.075. Class 16 is the highest at roughly 0.075. The red, orange and green bars mostly sit at 0.005–0.025, close to the LOSS baseline. In a few classes (2, 7, 10, 15) a competitor matches or exceeds the purple bar. Light dashed gridlines mark the y-axis ticks. The eye goes first to the tall purple bars, especially class 16.
caption: True positive rates at 1% false positive rate when each of 20 classes from CIFAR-100 (superclass set) are not seen at attack training time. Shadow model-based attacks struggle due to the lack of training samples, falling to near baseline performance (LOSS), while the quantile regression attack dramatically outperforms them by finding features that generalize across classes, including unseen classes.
abstract: A key tool in developing safe AI models is \emph{data auditing}, i.e., using statistical tools to determine whether harmful content may have been used in the training data of a black-box model. Unfortunately, most \emph{membership inference attacks} (MIAs) used to perform this type of auditing themselves assume \emph{access} to examples of harmful content from the same distribution as the query data. In real-world auditing scenarios, auditors often face legal and ethical restrictions preventing them from accessing a representative set of samples of harmful content to train MIA models effectively. We abstract and formalize this setting into a new data access model, the ``unseen class'' setting, and show that the state of the art MIAs fail due to the lack of access to the full target distribution. We show in this setting, \emph{quantile regression attacks} outperform approaches typically considered to be SoTA. We demonstrate this both empirically and theoretically, showing that quantile regression attacks achieve up to \textbf{11$\times$ the TPR} of shadow model-based approaches in practice, and providing a theoretical model that outlines the generalization properties required for this approach to succeed. Our work identifies an important failure mode in existing MIAs and provides a cautionary tale for practitioners that aim to directly use existing tools for real-world applications of AI safety.
